![What is a Biological Signature?](./cover.png)

A fingerprint identifies you from a patch of skin the size of a stamp. That is
the trick worth noticing: a few well-chosen features stand in for the whole
person, and you never need the person.

A biological fingerprint does the same job with molecules — a handful of genes,
proteins, or metabolites whose pattern pins down a state. This tumour and not
that one. Infected, not healthy. Measured rather than eyeballed, we call it a
**signature**.

## Finding one is feature selection

Assays are wide and cheap; patients are few and expensive. A microarray hands
you 20,000 genes on 70 people, nearly all of them noise for your question, and a
model handed all 20,000 will fit that noise perfectly. The signature is the short
list you keep.

1. **Measure wide.** Every feature on every sample.
2. **Find the groups.** Cluster if you don't know them yet; if you do, go
   straight to a classifier.
3. **Select.** Rank features by how well they separate the groups (*t*-test,
   mutual information), or let a sparse model do it for you (lasso, elastic net).
4. **Validate on data you never touched.** Redo the selection inside every
   cross-validation fold.

Step 4 is the whole ballgame. Select on all your data and the test set is already
contaminated: the genes were chosen *because* they separate those exact samples.
[Ambroise and McLachlan (2002)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.102102699) showed
this bias drives the apparent error rate towards zero, and that moving selection
inside each fold raises it sharply.

## The canonical example

[Golub and colleagues (1999)](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.286.5439.531)
measured 7,129 genes in bone marrow from 72 leukemia patients at the
Dana-Farber, chasing a question that decided treatment: is this ALL or AML? The
two look alike under a microscope, take opposite chemotherapies, and the call
rested on an expert's eye — accurate, but not reproducible between hospitals.
They clustered the samples and recovered both diseases *without being told they
existed*, then trained a 50-gene predictor. Fifty features out of 7,129: a
signature.

The same pipeline runs on eDNA reads to detect a jaguar from river water, and on
exoplanet spectra to flag an atmosphere that chemistry alone cannot hold. Wide
measurement, a short list, and an honest holdout.

**Further reading:** [Guyon and Elisseeff
(2003)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v3/guyon03a.html) on feature selection
generally; [Meinshausen and Bühlmann
(2010)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2010.00740.x) on keeping only the
features that survive resampling.
